summary: SWE-CC benchmarks coding agent compliance against 823 atomic policies from 12 open source repositories, finding agents violate 43.1% of applicable project governance policies even when functional unit tests pass.
implication: Confirms CIN's architecture where deterministic checker functions and structural validators enforce repo governance at every intermediate execution step rather than checking only final code.

title: Governance Architecture for Autonomous Agent Systems: Threats, Framework, and Engineering Practice
summary: Proposes the Layered Governance Architecture (LGA) for autonomous agents: sandboxing, intent verification, zero-trust inter-agent authorization, and immutable audit logging, evaluated on tool-call security benchmarks.
implication: Directly mirrors requirements for bounded agent runtime execution, inter-agent authorization boundaries, and tamper-evident audit logging.

title: Policy Cards: Machine-Readable Runtime Governance for Autonomous AI Agents
summary: Introduces Policy Cards as a machine-readable deployment-layer standard for operational, regulatory, and ethical constraints enforced on AI agents at runtime.
implication: Directly informs machine-checkable agent contracts and runtime policy enforcement schemas.

title: Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd
summary: Evaluating ensemble forecasting across Metaculus questions shows that diverse models with complementary errors outperform ensembles of correlated frontier models, even when individual models score lower.
implication: Observatory forecast aggregations should combine structurally diverse reasoning agents rather than sampling repeatedly from single frontier model families.

title: ForecastBench-Sim: A Simulated-World Forecasting Benchmark
summary: Introduces a simulated-world forecasting benchmark using Freeciv to generate fast, contamination-free questions across economics and strategy, revealing limits in frontier model reasoning over complex dynamics.
implication: Validates our simulation approach for testing forecasting and multi-agent dynamics without waiting months for real-world question resolution.

title: SPEAR: Five Principles for Interactive Human-Agent Alignment
summary: Reframes agent alignment from pre-deployment tuning to an ongoing interaction design problem across specification, process, evaluation, adaptation, and recalibration.
implication: Supports our design where agents regularly check in with people and allow ongoing calibration rather than relying purely on pre-trained obedience.

title: AI Safety Considerations for Agents With Limited Time to Act
summary: Proves that in partially observable environments with time limits, even an ideal agent cannot guarantee safety without explicit environmental constraints and bounded actions.
implication: Confirms that runtime safety must come from outside boundaries and structural limits on actions rather than relying solely on agent reasoning under time pressure.

title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents
summary: Agent Security Bench evaluates attacks and defenses across ten agent domains and 13 model backbones. Attacks on tool use and memory achieve up to 84% success, exposing severe weaknesses in current agent defense mechanisms.
implication: Autonomous tool execution requires hardened runtime policy enforcement points and strict isolation rather than relying on prompt-level defenses.

title: Delegated Misalignment: How Multi-Agent Structures Amplify LLM Safety Risks
summary: Testing six frontier models across 49 hazardous tasks shows multi-agent delegation amplifies execution of harm from 30.6% to 77.6% through responsibility diffusion and subordinate role compliance.
implication: Multi-agent simulations and agent runtimes cannot assume single-model alignment holds under delegation; structural monitors and bounded mortal compute contracts are strictly necessary.

title: ClarifyCodeBench: Evaluating LLMs on Clarifying Ambiguous Requirements for Code Generation
summary: Evaluates interactive ambiguity resolution with turn-discounted questioning and optimal round adherence, revealing that strong code generation does not guarantee effective clarification.
implication: Informs simulation benchmarks for the 'ask when it matters' harness: agents require explicit penalties for inefficient questioning and rewards for proactive ambiguity identification.

title: AgentPrivArena: Evaluating and Auditing Real-world AI Agent Privacy
summary: Introduces an evaluation and runtime auditing framework for AI agents using real tools, measuring intermediate data access to catch privacy leakage during multi-step execution.
implication: Supports our approach of auditing intermediate agent tool calls and data access rather than only checking final text outputs for privacy compliance.

title: Mi-Memory: A Lifecycle Memory Framework for Personal AI
summary: Proposes a lifecycle memory framework for personal AI assistants, emphasizing data continuity, local governance, and inspectable memory records across personal devices.
implication: Reinforces our twin architecture where personal memory is inspectable and kept under user authority rather than locked in remote platforms.

title: A Technical Taxonomy of LLM Agent Communication Protocols
summary: Taxonomy of nine open-source LLM agent communication protocols across five dimensions: counterparty, payload, interaction state, discovery, and schema flexibility. Predicts convergence toward a federated, layered protocol stack.
implication: Supports modular adoption of distinct layers: tool integration, session messaging, and peer delegation rather than a monolithic runtime.

title: A survey of agent interoperability protocols: Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A), and Agent Network Protocol (ANP)
summary: Compares emerging agent communication protocols MCP, ACP, A2A, and ANP across discovery, message format, and security, proposing a phased adoption roadmap from tool context to decentralized agent collaboration.
implication: Validates adopting established open protocols for tool contexts and structured agent delegation instead of proprietary custom transports.

title: Formal Runtime Verification for Tool-Using LLM Agents: An Offline Same-Benchmark Study on AgentDojo and STAC
summary: Replaying agent benchmark trajectories through metric first-order temporal logic monitors flags attack chains effectively, but uncovers that provenance-aware safety policies are vulnerable to spoofing unless provenance is strictly bound to the specific tool invocation.
implication: Agent runtime safety controls and trace monitors must cryptographically or structurally bind origin metadata to tool outputs rather than trusting agent-reported context.

title: Passing the Test You Trained On: Re-evaluating Prompt-Injection Detectors for LLM Agents
summary: Evaluating fifteen prompt injection detectors on agent benchmarks reveals that benchmark rankings fail to predict performance on real tool outputs, exhibiting high false-positive rates on benign tool returns.
implication: The network should not rely on general text prompt-injection benchmarks; containment defenses and filters must be evaluated on genuine agent tool outputs.
